bodyText: Maryland has no statute requiring background checks on apartment or property-management employees, including maintenance staff with access to units. Maryland employment law, not landlord-tenant law, governs any screening you choose to do.

title: Limits on Eviction Cost Shifting
bodyText: Your lease may not make the tenant responsible for the District Court summary ejectment filing surcharge assessed against you, and the court may not award it against a residential tenant. The one exception: the court may let you deduct the surcharge from the security deposit, up to the deposit amount, if you win possession and the lease says the surcharge may be assessed against the tenant. In a failure-to-pay-rent case, the judgment against a residential tenant covers rent, late fees and court costs, and only if the tenant was personally served. The statute lists lease-based attorney's fees only for nonresidential tenancies. Whether a residential lease attorney-fee clause can be enforced in some other proceeding is unsettled.

title: No Landlord Liability Waivers
bodyText: Any lease term whose effect is to indemnify you, hold you harmless, or excuse you from liability for injury, loss or damage caused by your own omission, fault, negligence or misconduct is void. This covers the premises and the elevators, stairways, hallways and other appurtenances not in the tenant's exclusive control. Your insurer cannot claim subrogation because the term is void. Tendering or trying to enforce such a term lets the tenant recover actual damages and attorney's fees.

title: When Rental Buildings Need Sprinklers
bodyText: Sprinkler systems are required in multifamily residential dwellings whose initial building permit was issued on or after July 1, 1990, and in town houses permitted on or after July 1, 1992, unless not served by public water. High-rise buildings, 4 or more stories or over 45 feet, built after July 1, 1974 also need a complete system, unless under 75 feet with qualifying fire-department aerial access. From October 1, 2026, a residential rental high-rise with an occupiable floor more than 75 feet above fire-department access must be fully sprinklered when it undergoes a substantial renovation permitted on or after that date. Substantial renovation means value-enhancing work costing at least 40% of the assessed building value. That renovation must also add the other listed fire-protection features.

title: High-Rise Fire Safety Information
bodyText: This applies if you own a residential high-rise with rental units, meaning 4 or more stories above grade or over 45 feet tall. Give fire safety and building evacuation information and instruction, including how to identify the fire alarm system elements, to new tenants when their occupancy starts and to existing tenants every 2 years. Each year, give all residents reasonable written notice that residents who are mobility impaired may ask for a unit on the first five floors if one becomes available. Equip all common means of egress with emergency escape lighting.

title: No Foreign-Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Maryland has no foreign-adversary or alien land law limiting who may own or lease residential property, and no lease-length carve-out to track. State law lets any alien who is not an enemy own, sell and deal with property as a citizen would. The meaning of the old 'enemy' limit has not been checked against case law.

title: No Fine Pass-Through Statute
bodyText: Maryland has no statute that specifically stops you from passing government fines on to tenants. However, your lease may not make a tenant give up any right or remedy, so a term making tenants pay fines for conditions you are responsible for could be challenged, and how far that goes is unsettled. Your lease may not penalize a tenant for calling police or emergency services. Counties and municipalities may not fine owners or tenants for those calls.

title: Immigration Status: What Applies
bodyText: Maryland has no statute that specifically bars landlords from asking about immigration status, and none that makes it unlawful to rent to someone without lawful status. National origin is a protected class, so status questions that single out applicants by national origin risk a discrimination claim. Condominium, homeowners association and cooperative boards may not require residents, guests or their children to give citizenship or immigration status as a condition of using recreational common areas. The same rule covers Social Security numbers, ITINs, birth certificates and similar information.

title: No Jury Trial Waiver
bodyText: Your residential lease may not make the tenant waive the right to a jury trial. A jury waiver in a lease of the tenant's primary residence is invalid and unenforceable. If either side demands a jury in an eviction case for nonpayment, holding over or breach, the court orders the tenant to pay rent as it comes due into a court escrow account, or to you if both agree, while the case is pending.

title: Liability for Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: A prohibited term in your lease is unenforceable. If you include one, the tenant may recover actual damages plus reasonable attorney's fees, and this covers terms barred by the lease-content statute, void liability waivers, and security deposit waivers. Liability arises if you tender the lease, try to enforce the term, or tell the tenant you intend to enforce it. No proof of knowledge is required, and there is no fixed penalty amount.

title: Written Lease Required (5+ Units)
bodyText: If you offer 5 or more dwelling units for rent in Maryland, you must use a written lease for each residential unit. If you do not, the tenancy is presumed to last 1 year from the tenant's first occupancy, and the tenant may end it earlier with 1 month's written notice. Every lease must contain the condition statement, each side's heat, gas, electricity, water and repair obligations, the security deposit receipt, and the current Maryland Tenants' Bill of Rights; the lease clauses handle those.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Maryland sets no minimum type size for residential leases, and no evidence rule penalizes small print. Type-size rules exist only for other contracts, such as motor vehicle leases, rent-to-own agreements and car rentals.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Maryland has no plain-language requirement for residential leases. Plain-language rules apply to other consumer documents, such as certain credit and car-rental forms. Misleading wording in a lease can still be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act.

title: Prohibited Residential Lease Terms
bodyText: Your lease may not: waive any right or remedy the law gives tenants; allow a shorter notice to quit than the law requires, though longer is allowed; or allow you to take possession or the tenant's belongings without court process unless the lease has ended and the property was abandoned. It also may not require tenants to accept rent-increase notices by electronic delivery, limit or penalize calling police or emergency services, or waive or condition the tenant's right of first refusal. Separate statutes also bar requiring the tenant to give longer notice to end the tenancy than you must give, and waivers of the security deposit, mitigation and utility-deduction rules. A ratio utility billing term is unenforceable unless you gave the required written disclosures first. Maryland has no specific ban on charging tenants home-warranty deductibles or routine repair fees, but whether such charges are a waiver of your repair duties is unsettled.

title: No General Applicant Inquiry Ban
bodyText: Maryland has no general statute barring landlords from asking applicants about protected characteristics, apart from the ban on discriminatory statements, notices and advertisements. Specific rules apply from October 1, 2026 if you own or manage 5 or more units, other than owner-occupied units. You may not ask about criminal history before a conditional offer except for listed serious convictions and sex-offender registration. You may not require drug or alcohol tests, and you may not ask applicants to release substance-use treatment program records.

title: No Owner-Occupancy Rental Limit
bodyText: Maryland has no statewide law limiting rentals of homes in single-family zones to owners who live on the lot. State policy encourages accessory dwelling units: each local legislative body must adopt a law allowing them by October 1, 2026. A deed, HOA or other recorded restriction may not unreasonably limit your ability to build or rent an accessory dwelling unit if you comply with applicable law, though limits on short-term rental of the unit are allowed. Local zoning rules on accessory units, including any owner-occupancy conditions, vary.

title: Applicant Criminal Records Confidentiality
bodyText: From October 1, 2026, if you own or manage 5 or more units (not owner-occupied), you may not give an applicant's criminal history records to anyone who will not use them to evaluate that applicant under Maryland's screening rules. You also may not use them for any other purpose, unless another law requires it. Violations carry a civil penalty of up to $500 each.

title: Tenant Organization Rights
bodyText: In an apartment building or complex of 4 or more units with a common landlord, not a single-family house, condominium or cooperative, a qualifying tenant organization of 3 or more resident tenants may use the tenant meeting room for its meetings during reasonable hours on reasonable notice. You may set reasonable terms that do not undermine that right, and you may require non-resident participants to sign a liability waiver. The first meeting each month must be free. Other meetings that month may carry a reasonable fee no higher than you charge other groups. You may not sue for possession, threaten eviction, arbitrarily raise rent, cut services or end a periodic tenancy because a tenant took part in a tenants' organization. A court may award the tenant up to 3 months' rent plus attorney's fees and costs.

title: Criminal Screening Notice Before Fee
bodyText: From October 1, 2026, if you own or manage 5 or more Maryland rental units (not owner-occupied), you must give applicants a written notice before accepting an application fee. The notice must explain how you use criminal history records checks, and state that the listed convictions may be considered only after a conditional offer. It must also tell applicants they may give you evidence of inaccuracies in their records, rehabilitation and mitigating factors. You must also tell applicants that an individualized assessment will be done. The Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs publishes a model notice for withdrawals of conditional offers.

title: Criminal-History Screening Rules
bodyText: From October 1, 2026, these rules apply if you own or manage 5 or more Maryland units, other than owner-occupied units, and if you check criminal history you must check every applicant. Before a conditional offer, you may ask only about listed convictions (such as sexual offenses, first- or second-degree murder, human trafficking, child pornography, and methamphetamine production in federally assisted housing) and sex-offender registration. After the offer you may also consider felonies within the 5 years before the application and listed convictions the applicant did not disclose. Withdraw only when necessary for a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, with a written specific reason and notice of the right to seek reassessment. If asked within 30 days, provide the records you relied on within 10 days. Renting to someone with a record, or not checking, cannot be the basis of a claim against you; violations carry a $500 civil penalty each, and local screening laws on this subject are preempted. Do not publish an ad saying you will not consider applicants who have been arrested or convicted, and keep your ads, signs, application forms and questions consistent with these rules, unless federal law requires otherwise.

title: No Lease Unconscionability Statute
bodyText: Maryland has no statute letting a court strike residential apartment or house lease terms as unconscionable. Statutory unconscionability rules cover leases of goods, mobile home park rental agreements and park rules, and timeshares. Whether courts apply common-law unconscionability to residential leases is unsettled. The specific lease-term bans in the landlord-tenant statutes still apply.

title: No Water Heater Setting Rule
bodyText: Maryland has no statute requiring you to set a water heater to a maximum temperature before a new tenant moves in. Lack of hot water is a serious defect for rent escrow and habitability purposes. Local housing codes and incorporated plumbing codes may set temperature limits.

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: Maryland has no statewide requirement to install window guards or give a window-guard lease notice. Window work for child safety arises under the lead law. For pre-1978 rentals, the modified risk reduction standard includes treating window sills, window wells and friction surfaces. Local housing codes may require more.

title: Rent Reporting: Existing Leases
bodyText: If you own six or more residential rental units in Maryland, you must offer tenants the option of having their on-time rent payments reported to at least one consumer reporting agency. For a lease entered into on or after October 1, 2026, the option goes in the written lease and the offer is repeated at least once a year. For a lease entered into before October 1, 2026, you must make the offer by January 1, 2027 and at least once a year after that, by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, by a tracked delivery service, or electronically if the tenant has elected electronic notices. Any fee is capped at the lesser of your actual cost or $10 a month.

title: Protecting Applicant and Tenant Data
bodyText: If you keep applicants' or tenants' names together with Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, financial account details or health information, protect them with reasonable security practices that fit the information and the size of your business. When you throw out applications or tenant files, take reasonable steps so no one can read or use the information, for example by shredding. If you share the information with a screening company or other vendor under a written contract, the contract must require the vendor to keep it secure. If your computer records are breached, investigate promptly and, unless misuse is unlikely, notify the Attorney General's office first and then the affected people within 45 days. Do not post or display Social Security numbers, and do not require an applicant to send one over the internet unless the connection is secure or the number is encrypted.

title: Landlord Cameras and Recording
bodyText: Do not place a camera, or have anyone place one, on a rental property to secretly watch people inside a tenant's home. Maryland makes this a crime punishable by up to 1 year in jail, a $2,500 fine or both. Owning the property is no defense, and the person watched can sue you for damages and attorney's fees. The rule does not cover a camera placed without the intent to watch people inside the home, such as one covering a parking lot, or a camera placed with an adult resident's consent. Recording a conversation, including a phone call with a tenant, is generally unlawful unless everyone in the conversation agrees in advance.

title: Dog Bites: Who Is Liable
bodyText: Maryland's dog-bite statute is aimed at the dog's owner. When a dog injures or kills someone, the owner is presumed to have known the dog was dangerous, and an owner is liable for injury or damage the dog causes while running at large, except to people who were trespassing, committing a crime or provoking the dog. For anyone else, including a landlord, liability follows the court-made rules as they stood on April 1, 2012, regardless of the dog's breed. The statute neither requires nor forbids breed limits in your pet policy; any limits you set must be stated in that policy.

title: Deadline to Sue a Former Tenant
bodyText: A suit for unpaid rent, damage or other money a former tenant owes under the lease generally must be filed within 3 years after the claim arises; a 12-year period applies to a contract under seal. Once the deadline passes you may not start a collection suit or arbitration. A payment or promise to pay after that point does not restart the clock, unless it is under a written payment plan signed before the deadline passed.

title: Counting Statutory Deadlines
bodyText: When a Maryland statute gives you or a tenant a number of days, such as the 45 days to return a deposit or the 10-day notice before filing for rent, do not count the day of the event that starts the period. Count the last day unless it is a Sunday or legal holiday; if it is, the period runs to the end of the next day that is not a Sunday or legal holiday. For periods of 7 days or less, skip Sundays and legal holidays in between; for longer periods, count them. If a court filing is due on a day the clerk's office is closed, file on the next full day it is open. These rules cover deadlines set by statute, not due dates your lease sets.

title: Property Managers and Licensing
bodyText: Maryland does not require a real estate license for an owner managing or leasing its own property. Collecting consumer debts for someone else generally requires a collection agency license, and the licensing law's exemption for collecting rent covers only licensed real estate brokers and people acting for them. Whether a manager who is not a broker needs a collection agency license to collect an owner's past-due rent is unsettled. A landlord's own regular employees may collect the landlord's own claims without one.

title: Why the Library Has No Arbitration Clause for Maryland
bodyText: Maryland's arbitration act makes a provision in a written contract to arbitrate future disputes valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds that would undo any contract (Md. Code Ann., Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-206(a)). The landlord-tenant law points the other way. You may not use a lease that has the tenant waive the right to a jury trial, or waive or forgo any right or remedy the law provides (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(d)(2), (4)), and a jury waiver in a lease of the tenant's primary residence is invalid and unenforceable (Real Prop. § 8-603(a)). An arbitration clause takes the disputes it covers away from a jury, so it could be read as exactly that kind of term. Guessing wrong is costly: if you offer a lease containing a prohibited provision, or try or threaten to enforce one, the tenant may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees, whether or not you knew the term was prohibited (Real Prop. § 8-208(g)(2)). Federal law may override the jury rule as applied to arbitration, but a court would decide that only after you had offered the lease, and Maryland case law was not reviewed. For that reason this library does not offer an arbitration clause for Maryland.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Maryland follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Md. Code, Com. Law § 3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Md. Code, Com. Law § 1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Maryland's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Real Property title 8 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Maryland's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: When Actual Notice Counts in Maryland
bodyText: Maryland's landlord-tenant law uses actual notice mainly for notices a tenant gives you. A tenant can start the rent-escrow and warranty-of-habitability remedies by a certified letter listing the defects, by actual notice of the defects, or by a written government violation notice (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-211(f)(2); § 8-212(f)(1)(ii)). The retaliation ban protects a tenant who gave you or a public agency written or actual notice of a good-faith complaint (§ 8-208.1(a)(2)(i)). And a tenant who pays rent to the former owner before actual notice of a transfer is discharged for that rent (§ 8-104). The landlord-tenant title does not define actual notice, and no statute lets you and the tenant agree on an extra method, such as text messages, for it. Maryland's commercial code defines notice and receipt for its own transactions only: a person has notice of a fact by actual knowledge, by receiving a notice, or by having reason to know it, and receives a notice when it comes to the person's attention or is delivered where the person holds out for such communications (Md. Code Ann., Com. Law § 1-202(a), (e)). The cautious course is to treat any report that actually reaches you or your manager, including a call, text or portal message, as notice. Your own notices must follow each statute's delivery rules; electronic delivery counts only where the statute allows it and the tenant elected it (Real Prop. § 8-209(b)(2); § 8-221(c)(3)).

title: Animals Left Behind in a Maryland Rental
bodyText: Maryland's animal cruelty law puts the care duty on anyone who has charge or custody of an animal, as owner or otherwise: that person may not unnecessarily fail to provide nutritious food, necessary veterinary care, proper drink, air, space, shelter and protection from the weather (Md. Code Ann., Crim. Law § 10-604(a)(5)). The statute sets no number of days after which a caretaker becomes the owner, but once you take charge of a tenant's pet, the cautious reading is that the duty is yours. An owner or custodian may not leave a domestic animal on private property intending to abandon it (§ 10-612(a)). At a court-ordered eviction, the sheriff or constable inspects for pets and gives them to the tenant, or, if the tenant is absent, calls an animal shelter or rescue and tells the tenant where the pet went; no one may put the pet out on public property (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 14-806). Maryland has no procedure for pets left in a unit the tenant has simply abandoned. Call local animal control rather than keeping or rehoming the animal yourself, and do not enter to care for a pet except as the entry statute allows (Real Prop. § 8-221).

title: No Statute on Professional Carpet Cleaning
bodyText: Maryland has no statute allowing or barring a lease requirement that the tenant pay for professional carpet cleaning at move-out, and no carpet-age or paint-age test. Deductions follow the general deposit rule: you may withhold only for unpaid rent, damage due to breach of the lease, and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear by the tenant or the tenant's family, agents, employees, guests or invitees (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-203(f)(1)(i)). The deposit is not liquidated damages and may be kept only to the extent you are actually damaged, and those rules cannot be waived in a lease (§ 8-203(f)(2), (l)). Any deduction needs an itemized statement with supporting documentation (§ 8-203(g)(1), (j)). The cautious course is to charge for cleaning only where carpet is soiled beyond ordinary wear, and to document the move-in condition.

title: Common-Area Electricity on a Tenant's Meter
bodyText: Maryland has no rule like Massachusetts' letting a lease make a tenant in a small building pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's meter. Two rules limit common-area charges. In a submetered apartment house (more than two units on a master meter), energy used in common areas and common facilities may not be billed to any occupant, and the lease must say common-area electricity or gas is your responsibility (COMAR 20.25.01.01F(1); COMAR 20.25.01.02B(3); COMAR 20.25.01.05A). And if you allocate a master-metered utility among tenants by ratio billing (2 or more units on a parcel), you must make the eight written disclosures first, including the allocation method (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-212.4(c)). If common lights in a two- or three-unit house run through one tenant's own utility account, the cautious course is to move them to a house meter or state the arrangement and its cost plainly in the lease and adjust the rent; whether that is enforceable is case law this library has not reviewed.

title: No Communal or Tribal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: Maryland has no communal, tribal or native-owned land whose leases need a government officer's approval, and no statute voiding leases of tribal land in the State. Leases of Maryland land follow the ordinary writing, recording and landlord-tenant rules. (The landlord-tenant and real property titles mention tribes only in the burial-site statute's definition of cultural affiliation, Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 14-121.)

title: Other Rules Maryland Does Not Have
bodyText: Some rules other states have are absent in Maryland. Maryland has no Proposition 65-style chemical warning duty, no work-card rule for staff of senior housing, no health-district rental rules to hand out, and no lease statement about shoreline access or special taxing districts. It has no student-housing licence or exemption, no Truth in Renting booklet (the Tenants' Bill of Rights fills that role), and no communal or tribal land lease approval. It has no statute on professional carpet cleaning, passing real estate tax increases to tenants, seasonal tenancies, employee housing, common-area lighting on a tenant's meter, or interrupting submetered utilities. It has no small-landlord exemption from rent escrow, no state rule splitting subsidy abatements, no end-of-term possession bond, no separate notice for nonrefundable fees, and no disaster-specific tenancy rules. Each is explained in its own row with what Maryland does have instead.

title: No Disaster-Specific Tenancy Rules
bodyText: Maryland has no statute that ends a tenancy, suspends rent or changes your duties after a declared natural disaster. The general casualty rule applies: if the rented improvements become untenantable by fire or unavoidable accident, a tenancy for a term of not more than 7 years ends and rent stops, prorated to the day of the fire or accident (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-112). Your duty to repair serious and dangerous defects, and the tenant's rent-escrow and warranty remedies, continue as usual (§§ 8-211, 8-212). Eviction courts may stay a warrant during extreme weather (§ 8-401(f)). Watch for emergency orders issued after a specific disaster, which may add temporary rules.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Maryland has not moved or renumbered the protection-order law that its abuse-victim lease protections rely on. The landlord-tenant subtitle for victims of abuse takes its definition of abuse from Md. Code Ann., Fam. Law § 4-501(b) (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-5A-01(b)), and that section is current: it covers acts causing serious bodily harm or fear of it, assault, rape or sexual offense, false imprisonment, stalking and revenge porn (Fam. Law § 4-501(b)(1)). The subtitle's qualifying court orders are a protective order under Fam. Law § 4-506 and a peace order under Md. Code Ann., Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-1505 whose underlying act was abuse (Real Prop. § 8-5A-02), and both sections are current. Use these citations when you review a tenant's request to end the lease early.

title: Energy Benchmarking and Tenant Data Consent
bodyText: If you own a commercial or multifamily residential building in Maryland of 35,000 square feet or more (excluding parking garage area), it is a covered building under the State's Building Energy Performance Standards (Md. Code Ann., Envir. § 2-1601(e)). Each year you must enter the prior year's benchmarking data into the benchmarking tool and report to the Department of the Environment by June 1, and you may use tenant energy data only to evaluate the building's performance (COMAR 26.28.02.02A-B). Electric and gas companies must give owners whole-building energy data for benchmarking (Envir. § 2-1602(d)). For a covered building with five or more tenants, the utility delivers whole-building data without individual tenant authorization (COMAR 26.28.02.04A(6)). For a covered building with fewer than five tenants, the utility delivers it only if the tenants consent in writing or electronically, and that consent may be given in a lease provision (COMAR 26.28.02.04A(7)). A tenant of a covered building must give you, within 30 days of your request, any benchmarking information you cannot get elsewhere (COMAR 26.28.02.03). If your covered building has fewer than five tenants, add a lease consent clause. The library does not offer a lease consent clause for this, since it matters only for covered buildings; if yours is one with fewer than five tenants, you can add your own clause.

title: Who May Represent an LLC or Corporation Landlord in Rent Court
bodyText: Maryland's lawyer-licensing statute lets any person represent a landlord in a summary ejectment or rent escrow proceeding in the District Court of Maryland, so an LLC or corporation landlord may appear there through a property manager or other agent who is not a lawyer (Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 10-206(b)(1)). For other District Court claims within the small-claim limit, an officer, member, partner or designated employee of the business may appear, but a designated employee must give the court a sworn power of attorney from the employer, may not be assigned full time to appear in court, and the business may not hire another business to provide appearance services (§ 10-206(b)(4)). Neither exception covers a circuit court appeal, so an entity landlord should expect to need a lawyer there. The Maryland Rules on appearances were not reviewed for this row; check the District Court's current rules and forms before relying on a non-lawyer.

title: Lease Termination After Well Contamination or Casualty
bodyText: Maryland gives no general landlord right to end a lease after an environmental public health event. Two statutes reach the subject. If a private well serving your residential rental tests above an EPA maximum contaminant level or a Department of the Environment harmful level, you must notify the Department and the local health department, provide an approved potable water supply until the contamination is permanently fixed, and within 60 days of learning of it resolve it, including by ongoing approved water, permanent remediation, or giving the tenant the option to end the lease (Md. Code Ann., Envir. § 9-4A-04(b)). That option is the tenant's, not yours. And if the rented improvements become untenantable by fire or unavoidable accident, a tenancy for a term of not more than 7 years ends and rent stops as of that day (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-112). A lease clause letting you terminate early after an environmental event would be a lease-based right only; the cautious course is to rely on the statutes and the lease's breach terms, and to keep any such clause from cutting the tenant's statutory rights (§ 8-208(d)(2)).

title: Faster Routes for Dangerous or Criminal Conduct
bodyText: Maryland has two faster routes for dangerous or criminal conduct. First, if the lease lets you repossess for a breach and the breach involves behavior by the tenant or someone on the property with the tenant's consent that shows a clear and imminent danger of serious harm to themselves, other tenants, you, your property or representatives, or anyone else on the property, you need give only 14 days' written notice instead of 30 before filing a breach-of-lease case (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-402.1(a)(1)(i)). The court still must find the breach substantial and warranting eviction, and either side may appeal within 10 days (§ 8-402.1(b)). Second, the State's Attorney, county attorney, a qualifying community association or a municipality can sue to abate a drug or prostitution nuisance; the case is heard within 14 days after service, and the court may order a tenant who knew or should have known of the nuisance to vacate within 72 hours and, if the tenant does not and you and the tenant are parties, order possession restored to you, with the warrant executed within 5 days (§ 14-120(g)(2), (h)(1), (l)). Maryland gives no eviction route that skips notice or a hearing.

title: Hunting on Rented Land in Maryland
bodyText: No one may hunt on land owned by another without the written permission of the landowner or the landowner's agent or lessee (Md. Code Ann., Nat. Res. § 10-411(a)). So a tenant of the land can lawfully give hunting permission. A hunter is liable for damage caused while hunting, and the landowner is not liable for accidental injury to the hunter whether or not the landowner or agent gave permission (§ 10-411(b)-(c)). Separately, a person may not wantonly enter another's cultivated land without permission from the owner or the owner's agent (Md. Code Ann., Crim. Law § 6-406). Maryland has no statute deciding whether a farm tenant gets hunting or fishing rights with the lease. If you want to keep or grant hunting rights, say so in the lease, including whether the tenant may permit others to hunt.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: In a Maryland failure-to-pay-rent case, a judgment for possession does not end the tenant's right to stay. The tenant may redeem the unit at any time before the eviction is actually carried out by paying you or your agent, in cash, certified check or money order, all past-due amounts the court determined plus all court-awarded costs and fees (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-401(h)(1)). A check issued by or on behalf of a government agency counts as the tenant's payment (§ 8-401(h)(2)). The right does not apply to a tenant against whom three judgments of possession for unpaid rent were entered in the 12 months before the case began (§ 8-401(h)(3)). Maryland has no separate forfeiture election or post-judgment redemption window for breach-of-lease or holdover cases. Your 6-day eviction notice must state the amount needed to redeem.

title: Codes Fixed to a Named Edition
bodyText: Some Maryland safety rules adopt an outside code at a named edition, so later editions do not apply until the State adopts them. The State Fire Prevention Code incorporates NFPA 1 Fire Code and NFPA 101 Life Safety Code, 2024 editions, and expressly excludes later tentative interim amendments and supplements unless the chapter specifically adopts them (COMAR 29.06.01.06). The Minimum Livability Code, which applies to rental housing where the locality has no conforming housing code, incorporates the 2012 International Property Maintenance Code with State modifications (COMAR 09.12.54.03; COMAR 09.12.54.04A). Submetered electricity must meet the meter standard the Public Service Commission incorporates by reference (COMAR 20.25.01.04A(2)). When a lease or your maintenance plan refers to a code, name the edition the State or your locality has adopted, not the latest one published.

title: What the Lease Can and Cannot Change About Condition
bodyText: A Maryland lease must state either that the premises will be made available in a condition permitting habitation with reasonable safety, 'if that is the agreement', or, if not, the actual agreement about the premises' condition (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(c)(1)). It must also state your and the tenant's specific obligations for heat, gas, electricity, water and repair (§ 8-208(c)(2)). That lets you agree on condition and assign routine duties. It does not let you contract out of the rent-escrow remedy or the warranty that a unit offered for rent is fit for human habitation, which exist by statute for all residential units except farm tenancies (§ 8-211(c); § 8-212(c)). A lease may not have the tenant waive any right or remedy the law provides (§ 8-208(d)(2)). One built-in limit: lack of heat, light, electricity or water is not a covered defect where the tenant is responsible for the utility and the lack is the direct result of the tenant's failure to pay (§ 8-211(d)(1)). Maryland has no rule letting a lease waive the water supply duty where there is no well or utility water.

title: Contamination Disclosures for Maryland Rentals
bodyText: Maryland has no general duty to disclose hazardous-substance contamination when you lease residential property. Two specific rules apply. If the rental is served by a private well, you must have the water tested every 3 years, give tenants the results, and tell each tenant the most recent results when the lease is signed (Md. Code Ann., Envir. § 9-4A-04(a)). And if the property is subject to a recorded environmental covenant under Maryland's environmental covenant law, the covenant runs with the land and may itself require notice when an interest in the property is transferred and impose activity and use limits (Md. Code Ann., Envir. §§ 1-802(b)(1), 1-804(a)). The statute does not require the covenant's terms to be copied into a residential lease, but a lease is an interest in the land, so read your covenant: if it limits uses (for example, groundwater use or digging) or requires notice to lessees, put those limits and notices in the lease.

title: No Health-District Rental Rules to Hand Out
bodyText: Maryland has no health districts that adopt rental regulations a landlord must give tenants on request, as Nevada's do. Housing standards are local. Where a county or city has not adopted a substantially conforming housing code, the State's Minimum Livability Code applies to rental housing (it excludes owner-occupied single-family homes), and the local political subdivision enforces it (COMAR 09.12.54.04A; COMAR 09.12.54.05A). Tenants complain to the local code or health office, and a written violation notice from a government agency counts as notice to you for rent escrow (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-211(f)(2)(iii)). Learn your county's or city's housing code and its complaint office.

title: Lead Registration Is the Only Statewide Rental Registration
bodyText: Maryland has no general statewide landlord registration. The one statewide registry is for lead: if you own a rental built before 1978 (an affected property), you must register each one with the Department of the Environment on its forms, listing your name and address, any property manager, your property or lead-hazard insurers and policy numbers, and a resident agent, other agent or contact person in Maryland, among other items (Md. Code Ann., Envir. § 6-811(b)). Renew by December 31 each year, update the owner, manager, insurer and agent details within 30 days of a change, and register within 30 days after acquiring an affected property (§ 6-812). Rental licensing and registration of all rentals are local: many counties and cities require them. Maryland has no rule requiring an out-of-state owner to hire a Maryland broker, and no State law barring local rental registration was found.

title: Maryland Late Fee Limits
bodyText: A Maryland residential lease may not provide a late-payment penalty above 5% of the unpaid rent due for the rental period that was late (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(d)(3)(i)). For a lease with weekly rent, the limit is $3 a week and $12 a month (§ 8-208(d)(3)(ii)). A provision over the limit is unenforceable, and offering or trying to enforce it exposes you to the tenant's actual damages and attorney's fees (§ 8-208(g)). Mobile home parks have their own rule: a park owner may charge a late fee only if the rental agreement provides for it, the fee does not exceed 5% of the rent due or $5, whichever is higher, and the rent is more than 5 days late (§ 8A-404). The rental park agreement must state the amount of any late fee (§ 8A-201(a)(3)(iii)). Ordinary residential leases have no statutory grace period.

title: Lead Inspection Certificate at Lease Signing
bodyText: For a Maryland rental built before 1978 (an affected property), when a lease is signed or a tenancy begins you must give the tenant the Department of the Environment's notice of tenant's rights together with a copy of the current verified inspection certificate for the property (Md. Code Ann., Envir. § 6-820(b), (d)). The certificate comes from an inspector accredited by the Department who is not related to you and who sends the verified report to the Department, you and the tenant (§ 6-818(a)). You must also give the rights notice again at least every 2 years, in writing by certified mail, return receipt requested, or another verifiable method the Department approves (§ 6-820(c), (e)(1)). Maryland has no separate requirement to attach the certificate to the lease as an exhibit, but attaching it and having the tenant acknowledge receipt is the easiest proof. Each affected property must also be registered with the Department and the registration renewed every year (§§ 6-811, 6-812).

title: Lease Terms the Tenant Must Initial
bodyText: Maryland has two lease terms that work only if the tenant separately marks them. An automatic renewal provision (other than one renewing for 1 month or less) must be set apart from the rest of the lease with a space for the tenant's written acknowledgment, and it is unenforceable by you unless it carries the tenant's initials, signature or witnessed mark (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(e)). And when you consent to a holdover, the tenant becomes month-to-month (or week-to-week, if the tenancy was weekly) unless the written lease states otherwise and the tenant initialed it (§ 8-402(d)). No Maryland statute requires initials for a longer notice period or for any other lease term. Have the tenant initial each of these provisions next to its text.

title: Recording a Maryland Lease
bodyText: Most Maryland residential leases need not be recorded. Recording is required for an estate above seven years, but not for a lease with an initial term of seven years or less where each renewal term is also seven years or less and a party controls whether it renews (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 3-101(a), (c)). Even a lease that should have been recorded and was not is still valid between the original parties, against their creditors, and against anyone claiming through a party who acquires an interest with actual notice of the lease or while the tenant is in such actual occupancy as to give reasonable notice (§ 3-101(d)). A memorandum of lease signed by every party may be recorded instead of the full lease (§ 3-101(e)). A lease is sufficient without acknowledgment (§ 4-101(a)(2)). Recording changes no landlord-tenant right. For ordinary residential leases, keep the signed lease and make sure the tenant is in possession; record a memorandum only for a long lease or one with an option to buy.

title: Lease Length and Signatures in Maryland
bodyText: A Maryland lease created orally, and not in a writing signed by the party creating it or that party's agent authorized in writing, has the effect of a tenancy at will only (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 5-101). That rule does not apply to a lease for a term of one year or less (§ 5-102). A lease for an estate above seven years must be executed and recorded, with the renewal exception for leases of seven years or less (§ 3-101(a), (c)). A lease is sufficient without acknowledgment, and no seal is required (§ 4-101(a)(2), (b)). Separately, if you offer 5 or more dwelling units for rent in Maryland you must use a written lease, and if you do not, the tenancy is presumed to run 1 year from first occupancy unless the tenant ends it earlier on 1 month's written notice (§ 8-208(a)). No Maryland statute in the property titles requires a spouse's consent or joinder for a lease of more than a year; if the property is owned jointly, including by spouses, have every owner sign.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages: Three Years
bodyText: A suit against a tenant or former tenant for unpaid rent, damage or other money owed under an ordinary lease must be filed within 3 years after the claim accrues (Md. Code Ann., Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-101). A 12-year period applies to a contract under seal or other specialty, and a payment on a specialty suspends that period for 3 years (§ 5-102(a), (b)). For a consumer debt, once the period runs you may not start a collection action, and a later payment, promise or other activity on the debt does not revive or extend it, except under a separate written payment plan the tenant entered before the period ran (§ 5-1202). The tenant's claims have their own limits: a suit over an excess security deposit may be brought during the tenancy or within 2 years after it ends (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-203(b)(4)). Maryland's landlord-tenant title sets no shorter deadline for your suit against a former tenant. Sue promptly after move-out, and do not count on a partial payment to keep an old claim alive.

title: No Lockouts for Late Rent
bodyText: Maryland does not allow a lockout for unpaid rent, so the library offers no lock-change clause for Maryland. You may not take or threaten to take possession of a dwelling unit by locking the tenant out, by any other action, or by intentionally interrupting heat, running water, hot water, electricity or gas to force the tenant out (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-216(a)(3), (b)(1)). You may take possession only under a court warrant of restitution executed by a sheriff or constable, or after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit (§ 8-216(b)(2)). A tenant who wins can recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees and costs (§ 8-216(c)(1)). For unpaid rent, use the failure-to-pay-rent case after the required 10-day notice.

title: Shifting Maintenance to the Tenant in Maryland
bodyText: Your Maryland lease must spell out your and the tenant's specific obligations for heat, gas, electricity, water and repair of the premises (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(c)(2)). That is where you assign routine maintenance, yard work or minor repairs to the tenant. The statute requires no separate writing, no specific consideration and no rent reduction for the shift. You cannot shift your obligation to repair serious and dangerous defects or the warranty of habitability, because the lease may not have the tenant waive a right or remedy the law provides (§ 8-208(d)(2); § 8-211(d); § 8-212(c)). Write each assigned task specifically, and keep structural, utility-system and safety repairs with you.

title: No Separate Notice Rule for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: Maryland has no rule requiring a separate written notice when you collect a nonrefundable deposit or fee. A Maryland security deposit, which includes prepaid last month's rent, can never be nonrefundable: it is not liquidated damages and may be kept only for unpaid rent and actual damage (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-203(a)(3), (f)(2)), and those rules cannot be waived in a lease (§ 8-203(l)). The only statutory disclosure of nonrefundable charges is the pet policy, which must list any up-front nonrefundable pet fees, refundable pet deposits and monthly pet fees, linked on the property's website if any and summarized in the rental application (§ 8-210(c)). State any other nonrefundable fee in the lease, and keep it out of the security deposit.

title: Where Maryland Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several Maryland rules work only if your lease opts in. To repossess for a breach before a fixed term ends, the lease must say you may repossess if the tenant breaches it (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-402.1(a)(1)(i)). An automatic renewal clause (other than for 1 month or less) must be set apart and carry the tenant's initials, signature or witnessed mark (§ 8-208(e)). A holdover becomes month-to-month (or week-to-week) unless the written lease, initialed by the tenant, says otherwise (§ 8-402(d)). A deposit of up to 2 months' rent is allowed only for a tenant qualified for State utility assistance who pays utilities to you, with the amount agreed in writing (§ 8-203(b)(2)). The tenant may agree in writing to entry on less than 24 hours' notice (§ 8-221(c)(5)). Electronic delivery of rent-increase and entry notices works only if the tenant elects it, and you may not make that election a condition of the application (§ 8-209(b)(2); § 8-221(c)(3)). If you own 6 or more units, the lease must offer positive rent reporting, which the tenant may accept (§ 8-208.4(b)-(c)). If you add an option to buy, the agreement must carry the statutory capital-letter statements or the tenant may void it (§ 8-202). Leaving out an opt-in term leaves you with the statute's default.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond; Appeal Bonds Only
bodyText: Maryland has no statutory bond a tenant gives to secure surrender at the end of the term, and a residential lease may not have the tenant authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(d)(1)). The bonds in a Maryland eviction are appeal bonds. A tenant who appeals a failure-to-pay-rent judgment must give you a bond with sureties to stay execution (§ 8-401(i)(2)). A tenant who appeals a holdover or breach-of-lease judgment keeps possession only by filing an affidavit that the appeal is not for delay, filing a sufficient bond and paying rent in arrears and costs (§ 8-402(b); § 8-402.1(b)(2)). A surety bond the tenant buys instead of a security deposit is a separate device governed by the deposit statute (§ 8-203(i)). Do not put a possession bond or confessed judgment in a Maryland lease.

title: No Chemical-Exposure Warning Law Like California's
bodyText: Maryland has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65: no statute requires a landlord to post or give a warning about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. The Maryland disclosures that do touch hazards in rentals are specific: lead for pre-1978 rentals, private well test results, mold information and the high-rise sprinkler notice. Follow those, and the federal lead-based paint disclosure.

title: No Small-Landlord Escape from Rent Escrow
bodyText: Maryland has no notice that lets a small landlord opt out of rent escrow. Rent escrow covers all residential dwelling units leased for human habitation in the State, public or private, single or multiple, and excludes only farm tenancies (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-211(c)). The warranty of habitability reaches the same units (§ 8-212(b)). So a one-unit landlord is covered the same as a large one, and no lease notice changes that.

title: Maryland Required Lease Disclosures and When They Are Due
bodyText: Maryland's required lease contents and disclosures are spread across several laws. In every lease: the condition statement, each party's obligations for heat, gas, electricity, water and repair, the security deposit receipt, and the current Tenants' Bill of Rights (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(c)); and, in the lease or on a posted sign, the name, address and phone number of you or your agent for notices and service (§ 8-210(a)). At signing: the mold pamphlet (§ 8-220(b)); for pre-1978 rentals, the lead rights notice and current inspection certificate (Md. Code Ann., Envir. § 6-820(b), (d)); for private wells, the latest water test results (Envir. § 9-4A-04(a)(3)). Before the lease: utility billing disclosures when tenants pay you or a third party for utilities, or you use ratio billing (Real Prop. §§ 8-205.1-8-205.3, 8-212.4). Maryland requires no statewide notice of rent-control or just-cause coverage, and no State form must be the lease's first page. Adding an option to buy changes the picture for a single-family property of four or fewer units: the lease option must carry the capital-letter statements of § 8-202, and you must give the tenant the State Real Estate Commission's residential property disclosure or disclaimer statement before the tenant signs a lease containing the option, with a signed, dated acknowledgment attached (§ 10-702(b)(1), (c), (f)(3)-(4)). A purchaser who does not get it may rescind, and in a lease with option the right to terminate ends at occupancy (§ 10-702(h), (k)(2)(ii)).

title: Maryland's Tenants' Bill of Rights and Other Required Hand-Outs
bodyText: Maryland's state-published rights guide is the Maryland Tenants' Bill of Rights. Every lease must include a copy of its most current version, published by the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs in the Department of Housing and Community Development (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(c)(4)). The Office publishes it on its website by June 1 each year, summarizing tenants' rights and remedies under State and federal law (Md. Code Ann., Hous. & Cmty. Dev. § 5-104(a)(1), (c)). Maryland requires no separate signed acknowledgment of it and no re-delivery at renewal, but a renewal lease must include it like any lease. Two other State hand-outs apply: give each tenant the Department of the Environment's mold pamphlet at signing and on request, and ask the tenant to sign an acknowledgment of receipt (Real Prop. § 8-220(b)); and if you know the tenant has a pet, include with the lease a link to the Department of Agriculture's pets-and-eviction fact sheet (§ 14-804). Download the current Bill of Rights each time you sign or renew a lease.

title: Waivers of the Minimum Livability Code
bodyText: Maryland has no state sanitary code, but where a locality has not adopted its own conforming housing code, rental housing is subject to the State's Minimum Livability Code (COMAR 09.12.54.04A). The local political subdivision may waive the Code, in whole or part, for a rental unit on the owner's application only if the tenant gets adequate notice in the form the locality specifies, has a chance to comment in writing or in person, and the waiver would not threaten the tenant's health or safety (COMAR 09.12.54.05B(1)). A locality may also waive it based on the occupant's religious practices (COMAR 09.12.54.05B(2)). Nothing requires a granted waiver to be attached to the lease. If you hold one, the cautious course is to give each new tenant a copy at signing, since the tenant's right to notice of the application suggests the waiver should not be hidden. Local housing codes may have their own variance procedures.

title: No Special Rules for Seasonal Leases
bodyText: Maryland has no seasonal-tenancy statute: a summer or vacation lease ends the way any other lease does. The notice-to-quit rule covers tenancies at the end of a stated term, so for a written lease for a stated term of more than 1 week you must give written notice 60 days before the term ends to repossess if the tenant stays (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-402(c)(1)-(2)). Seasonal rentals are exempt from the application-fee refund rule (§ 8-213(c)). Counties and cities may regulate short-term rentals, meaning a unit used for housing for less than 31 consecutive days (§ 14-126(a)(6), (b)(5)). For a seasonal lease longer than a week, send the 60-day notice to quit when you sign or well before the season ends, and check local short-term rental and tax rules.

title: Returning the Security Deposit in Maryland
bodyText: Within 45 days after the tenancy ends, return the security deposit with simple interest, less any damages rightfully withheld (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-203(e)(1)). Interest is due only on deposits of $50 or more held at least 6 months, at the greater of the 1-year Treasury yield curve rate or 1.5% a year (§ 8-203(e)(1)-(3)). You may withhold only for unpaid rent, damage due to breach of the lease, and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear by the tenant or the tenant's family, agents, employees, guests or invitees (§ 8-203(f)(1)(i)). If you withhold anything, mail the tenant, first-class to the last known address within the same 45 days, a written list of damages with an itemized statement of the costs, including supporting documentation; if you use an estimate, send the final invoice when the work is done and refund any excess within 30 days (§ 8-203(g)(1), (j), (k)). Missing the list forfeits your right to withhold for damages (§ 8-203(g)(2)). Withholding without a reasonable basis exposes you to up to three times the amount withheld plus attorney's fees (§ 8-203(e)(4)). A tenant who was evicted or abandoned the unit before the tenancy ended must first demand the deposit in writing within 45 days, giving a new address; you then have 45 days from that notice (§ 8-203(h)). None of this can be waived in a lease (§ 8-203(l)).

title: No Work Cards for Staff in Senior Housing
bodyText: Maryland has no requirement that staff of housing for older adults hold a work card or similar permit, as Nevada requires. The State's senior-housing rule in the landlord-tenant title concerns conversions: a landlord of a senior apartment facility that will stop operating as one owes its tenants advance notice and relocation help (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-217). Screen employees under your own policy and fair employment law.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure in a Maryland Lease
bodyText: Maryland has no rule requiring a lease to disclose shoreline or beach access, as Rhode Island does. The closest rule applies to sales only: a contract for the sale of real property must carry a notice that the property may be in the Chesapeake and Atlantic Coastal Bays Critical Area, where extra land-use rules apply (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 14-117(d)). If you advertise water access with a waterfront rental, describe exactly what access the tenant gets and any association or easement limits in the lease.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings Needs the Tenant's Writing
bodyText: Maryland lets you enter to show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, lenders, tenants or contractors (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-221(a)(3)). Outside an emergency, you must give written notice at least 24 hours ahead stating the date, approximate time and specific purpose, and enter only between 7:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m., Monday through Saturday, unless the tenant agrees in writing to another time (§ 8-221(b)-(c)). A tenant may agree in writing to an entry on less than 24 hours' notice (§ 8-221(c)(5)). The statute does not require a separate document for that agreement, does not distinguish showings to buyers from showings to tenants, and does not let the tenant waive notice altogether. Because a lease may not have the tenant give up any right the law provides (§ 8-208(d)(2)), the cautious course is to get a dated, signed agreement for the specific showing period or showings you have in mind, and still give notice of each entry, instead of relying on a general lease waiver.

title: No Special District Statement Required in a Maryland Lease
bodyText: Maryland requires no lease statement about special taxing districts or similar districts. District-type charges are disclosed only in sale contracts: for example, deferred water and sewer charges must be disclosed in a contract for the initial sale or resale of residential property (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 14-117(a)). Those are the owner's obligations. If your lease passes any district, association or deferred charge to the tenant, state the charge and amount in the lease.

title: Maryland's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Maryland caps these lease charges. Security deposit: 1 month's rent per unit, or up to 2 months for a tenant qualified for State utility assistance who pays utilities to you, if agreed in writing (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-203(b)); a surety bond plus deposit may not exceed 2 months' rent (§ 8-203(i)(3)). Late fee: 5% of the unpaid rent for the period, or $3 a week and $12 a month for weekly rent (§ 8-208(d)(3)). Up front: no more than the deposit plus the first month's rent to start the lease (§ 8-208(d)(11)). Application fees over $25: refund all but what you actually spent on credit checks and other application costs within 15 days, unless you offer 4 or fewer units on one parcel or at one location (§ 8-213(b)-(c)). Eviction warrant notice cost: up to $5 (§ 8-407). Positive rent reporting: up to the lesser of your cost or $10 a month (§ 8-208.4(h)(1)). Dishonored check: after the statutory notice, a collection fee of up to $35 (Md. Code Ann., Com. Law § 15-802(b)). Submetered electricity or gas: the utility's actual charges plus up to $1 per unit per month (Md. Code Ann., Pub. Util. § 7-303(d)(2)). Mobile home parks: a late fee of up to 5% of rent or $5, whichever is higher (Real Prop. § 8A-404). Counties and cities may add limits, including rent limits.

title: No Special Rules for Renting to Students
bodyText: Maryland's landlord-tenant law has no student-housing licence, certification or disclosure and no student exemption. Renting to students follows the ordinary rules. The only statutory mention is in the local short-term-rental rule, which excludes a group residential facility for students, fraternity or sorority house from its definition of short-term rental unit (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 14-126(a)(6)(ii)). Some cities near campuses regulate student rentals by local ordinance, so check local law.

title: No State Rule Splitting Subsidy Abatements
bodyText: Maryland has no statute prorating or splitting rent between a subsidized tenant and a housing agency when a unit fails a habitability inspection. A tenant's state-law remedy for serious defects is rent escrow, where the court may abate the rent required by the lease by an amount it finds fair (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-211(m)), and the warranty of habitability (§ 8-212). Abatement of housing assistance payments for a voucher unit that fails inspection is governed by federal HUD rules and your housing assistance payments contract, not Maryland law. Keep the agency's inspection results and abatement notices with the lease file.

title: No Statute on Passing Tax Increases to Tenants
bodyText: Maryland has no statute on residential lease clauses that pass real estate tax increases to the tenant, and the deposit law gives no right to deduct a share of a tax increase. A mid-term increase in what the tenant pays is a rent increase: it needs a lease term allowing it and the written notice the rent-increase statute requires, at least 90 days ahead for a term over 1 month (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-209(b)). Security deposit deductions are limited to unpaid rent and damage (§ 8-203(f)(1)(i)). The cautious course for a residential lease is to fix the rent for the term and raise it at renewal with proper notice.

title: No Employee-Housing Rules in Maryland Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: Maryland's landlord-tenant law has no rule for housing you provide to an employee: no required disclosure of occupancy and vacating terms, no offer of a rental agreement when the job ends, and no special eviction route for caretakers or resident managers. If the employee pays rent or occupancy is part of pay, treat the arrangement as a tenancy and use a written lease with the required Maryland contents (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(c)), ending it with the notice the statute requires (§ 8-402(c)). If someone stays with no right to possession and no landlord-tenant remedy applies, the wrongful detainer action is the route (§ 14-132). Farm-worker housing may have separate health and labor rules not covered here. State in writing that the housing ends with the job and how much notice applies.

title: Changing Terms Mid-Tenancy in Maryland
bodyText: Maryland's only statutory notice rule for changing a residential tenancy's terms is the rent-increase rule. You must notify the tenant in writing before raising rent: at least 90 days ahead for a term of more than 1 month, 60 days for more than 1 week but not more than 1 month (such as month-to-month), and 7 days (written lease) or 21 days (no written lease) for 1 week or less (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-209(b)(1), (b)(3)). Send it by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, or electronically if the tenant elected that (§ 8-209(b)(2)). The rule does not apply once you have given notice to terminate the tenancy, and local law may require more (§ 8-209(a)(2), (c)). No statute sets a separate notice for raising a fee the lease already provides or for changing other terms of a periodic tenancy. During a fixed term you need the tenant's agreement to change the lease. For a periodic tenancy, the cautious course is to treat a new fee or other changed term like a rent increase, giving the § 8-209 notice period, or to end the tenancy with the notice § 8-402(c) requires and offer a new lease (§ 8-402(c)(2)). Whether a fee increase counts as a rent increase under § 8-209 is case law this library has not reviewed.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Maryland's trespass law lets you, as owner or through your agent, tell a non-tenant not to enter or to leave your private property. A person may not enter or cross private property after the owner or the owner's agent has told the person not to, unless entering under a good-faith claim of right or ownership, and may not remain after being told to leave (Md. Code Ann., Crim. Law § 6-403(a)-(b)). The section prohibits only wanton entry (§ 6-403(d)). Property posted against trespass with conspicuous signs is also protected (§ 6-402(a)). The statute has no landlord-specific rule. A tenant's guest or invitee is on the property under the tenant's right of possession, so banning a tenant's guest from the tenant's own unit is risky; limit a trespass notice to common areas you control, give it in writing, keep a copy, and do not use it against people the tenant is entitled to receive, such as emergency or service providers. Whether a landlord's ban binds a tenant's invitee in common areas is case law this library has not reviewed.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Booklet; the Tenants' Bill of Rights Instead
bodyText: Maryland has no Truth in Renting statement or act like New Jersey's or Michigan's. Its counterpart is the Maryland Tenants' Bill of Rights: every lease must include a copy of the most current version published by the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs in the Department of Housing and Community Development (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(c)(4)). A lease must also include the condition statement, each party's utility and repair obligations and the security deposit receipt (§ 8-208(c)(1)-(3)). Download the current version before each signing.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Maryland)
bodyText: Maryland is a common-law state and has no usufruct. The nearest status is a life estate. A life tenant, like any tenant for years or other possessor, is liable for actual damages for waste committed or permitted without authorization (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 14-102(a)). Where one person holds a life estate and others hold remainder interests, a court of equity may, on application of a party and with all living parties joined, decree a lease (or sale or mortgage) if it is advantageous, and direct the rent to the people who would be entitled to it (§ 14-110(a)). No Maryland statute says what happens to a lease granted by a life tenant when the life tenant dies; that is case law this library has not reviewed, and the cautious assumption is that the lease may not bind the remainder holders. If you lease property you hold for life, tell the tenant in writing, have the remainder holders join the lease, or seek a court decree.

title: Utility Cost Disclosures Before the Lease
bodyText: Maryland prescribes no stand-alone utility attachment form, but several utility arrangements need written disclosures, and the lease charge fails without them. If you bill tenants for water, sewer, gas or electricity yourself, the written lease must say the tenant pays you for that utility; in a building of 6 or more units you must also either give copies of the bills or, before the lease and each renewal term, state the prior year's total cost by utility, and in a building of 5 or fewer you must give copies of the bills (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. §§ 8-205.1(c), 8-205.2(c)). If the tenant pays a third party for submetered water or sewer, the lease must say so, you must give a copy of each bill at least 20 days before it is due, and before the first lease you must state the unit's water and sewer costs for the prior 2 years (or a comparable unit's) (§ 8-205.3(b)). If you allocate master-metered utilities by ratio billing with 2 or more units on a parcel, you must give prospective tenants eight written items, including the last two utility bills, the allocation method and the prior year's average monthly bill; without them, the lease's billing provision is unenforceable (§ 8-212.4(c); condominiums and cooperatives excluded, § 8-212.4(b)). Maryland has no rule requiring you to give a prospective tenant past heating or cooling bills when the tenant pays the utility directly.

title: No Right to Cut Off Submetered Utilities
bodyText: Maryland has no procedure letting a landlord interrupt submetered electricity or gas for nonpayment. The Public Service Commission's submetering rules cover meters, billing and records, but say nothing about disconnection, and an occupant of a submetered apartment house is not a customer of the utility and has no complaint rights before the Commission; bill disputes are between you and the occupant and go to the local complaint agency (COMAR 20.25.01.07). You may not intentionally interrupt heat, running water, hot water, electricity or gas to force a tenant out (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-216(a)(3), (b)(1)). Your submetered lease must state that the building is submetered, that bills follow the submeter readings and that common-area energy is your responsibility (COMAR 20.25.01.02B). Bills are past due if not paid within 20 days of mailing (COMAR 20.25.01.05F(3)). Collect unpaid submeter charges as a debt under the lease, not by cutting service.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing in Maryland
bodyText: Maryland requires your key notices to be written, and a lease cannot downgrade them, because it may not have the tenant waive a right the law provides (Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-208(d)(2)). In writing: a rent increase (§ 8-209(b)(1)); the 10-day notice of intent to file a failure-to-pay-rent case, on the Judiciary's form (§ 8-401(c)(1)-(2)); the notice to quit ending a tenancy (§ 8-402(c)(2)); the 30-day or 14-day notice of breach before a breach-of-lease case (§ 8-402.1(a)(1)(i)); and the 24-hour entry notice (§ 8-221(c)(1)). The tenant's notices that start deposit rights go by certified mail (§ 8-203(f)(1)(ii)). An abuse victim's notice ending the lease is written (§ 8-5A-02(b)). One exception runs the other way: outside Baltimore City, if a tenant gives you oral notice of moving out at least 30 days ahead (90 days for year-to-year, 180 for farms) and you can prove it by testimony, you need not send your own written notice to quit (§ 8-402(c)(3)). Electronic delivery counts as written only where the statute allows it and the tenant elected it.
